Precautions: Use with caution. Seed oil is intended primarily for external use and may cause skin irritation or allergic reactions. Avoid internal use without professional guidance and ensure proper plant identification.
Botany: Bilogo is a smooth woody vine, reaching a length of 4 to 10 meters. Branches are pendulous. Leaves are ovate to elliptic-ovate, 5 to 12 centimeters long, toothed at the margins. Flowers are numerous, greenish or greenish white, borne on lax, pendulous panicles, 7 to 18 centimeters long and about 5 millimeters in diameter. Fruit is ovoid or subglobose, 7 to 9 millimeters long, yellow, three-celled and usually three-seeded. Seeds are red and surrounded by a fleshy aril.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for skin diseases, intestinal worms, joint pain, rheumatism, and certain digestive ailments after proper detoxification.
Preparation: The tuber is carefully processed through repeated slicing, soaking, washing, and cooking to remove its natural toxins before use. It may also be prepared as a traditional poultice for external application.
Precautions: Use with extreme caution. The raw tuber is highly poisonous and contains toxic compounds that can cause dizziness, vomiting, difficulty breathing, paralysis, or death if consumed without proper detoxification. Do not consume raw. Use only after correct traditional processing and with expert guidance.
Botany: Nami is a twining vine, arising from tuberous roots, and reaching a length of several meters. Stems covered with few or many short, sharp spines. Leaves are 3-foliolate, the leaflets 12 to 20 centimeters long, somewhat hairy, the lateral ones oblique, oblong-ovate, the terminal one equilateral, oblong to oblong-obovate. Panicle is axillary, slender, hairy, 12 to 20 centimeters long. Flowers are small; unisexual male flowers with 6 stamens; female flowers similar to males, 3-winged, 3-celled, ovules 2 in each cell. Fruit is a capsule, oblong and about 5 centimeters long. Flesh and sap of tubers are yellowish.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for diarrhea, dysentery, wounds, skin infections, inflammation, and minor bleeding.
Preparation: The bark and leaves are commonly prepared as a decoction for internal use or applied externally as a poultice or wash for wounds and skin conditions.
Precautions: Use with caution. Excessive internal use may cause digestive discomfort. Avoid use during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless advised by a qualified healthcare professional. Ensure proper plant identification before use.
Botany: Kolis is a smooth shrub or small tree reaching a height of 8 meters. Leaves are leathery, oblong-ovate to oblong elliptic, 6 to 14 centimeters long, green, shining, and usually pointed at both ends. Flowers are faintly scented, numerous, about 7 millimeters across, deep blue or purple, and borne on axillary, solitary or fascicled cymes, 2 to 4 centimeters long. Fruit is rounded, 7 to 10 millimeters diameter, fleshy and dark purple.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for diarrhea, dysentery, stomach discomfort, wounds, skin infections, inflammation, and toothache.
Preparation: The bark is commonly prepared as a decoction for internal use, while the bark or leaves may also be used as a wash or poultice for wounds and skin conditions.
Precautions: Use with caution. Excessive internal use may cause digestive discomfort due to its high tannin content. Avoid use during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless advised by a qualified healthcare professional. Ensure proper plant identification before use.
Botany: Cyrtophyllum fragrans is a tree up to 30 m tall, growing irregularly shaped, with deeply fissured dark bark, and with buttress roots up to 2.5 m tall. Branches are distinctive, extending outwards and upwards like fingers. Leaves are opposite, oval-shaped, light green; stalked leaves have thinly leathery to leathery leaf blades that are usually elliptic, distinctly tipped, and 5–13 by 2–5.5 cm.. Flowers are bisexual in 4–12 cm wide flowering clusters (inflorescence) that develop at the leaf axils; cream-white turning yellow, fragrant, and about 2 cm across. Fruits are orange or red, broadly ellipsoid, bitter tasting, containing numerous tiny seeds of less than 1 mm.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for fever, diarrhea, stomach disorders, inflammation, wounds, and minor skin infections.
Preparation: The bark and leaves are commonly prepared as a decoction for internal use or applied externally as a wash or poultice for wounds and skin conditions.
Precautions: Use with caution. Scientific evidence supporting its medicinal use is limited. Avoid excessive consumption and use during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless advised by a qualified healthcare professional. Ensure proper plant identification before use.
Botany: Igiu is a tree reaching a height of 10 to 20 meters. Leaves are crowded at the ends of the branches, 20 to 60 centimeters long, pinnate with 10 or more pairs of leaflets. Lower leaflets are usually ovate, less than 10 centimeters long; the median and upper ones are oblong, 20 centimeters or more in length. Flowers are pale yellowish, hairy, about 1 centimeter long, 5-parted, borne in axillary drooping panicles which are about 40 centimeters long. Fruit is yellow, hairy, depressed-globose, about 1.5 to 2 centimeters in diameter, containing red seeds.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for cough, colds, asthma, stomachache, indigestion, diarrhea, joint pain, inflammation, and mild bacterial infections.
Preparation: The leaves are commonly prepared as a decoction, infused as herbal tea, eaten fresh, or crushed and applied externally to affected areas.
Precautions: Use with caution. Excessive consumption may cause stomach irritation in sensitive individuals. Avoid medicinal use during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless advised by a qualified healthcare professional. Ensure proper plant identification before use.
Botany: Kayetana is a small or medium-sized tree reaching a height of 20 meters. Branchlets are usually spineless. Bark has prominent conical spines. Leaves are pinnately compound, up to 35 centimeters or more in length, with 8 to 20 pairs of leaflets which are somewhat ovate, 5 to 12 centimeters long, with two sides very unequal, particularly at the base, with a tapering, pointed tip. Flowers are numerous, fairly small, yellowish-white, with a red center, 4-parted, and borne in considerable number on terminal panicles which are about 40 centimeters long. Fruit is solitary, 6 to 8 millimeters in diameter, finely tubercled, and red when ripe. Seeds are somewhat rounded, and bluish-black.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for wounds, skin infections, inflammation, fever, and digestive discomfort.
Preparation: The leaves and bark are commonly prepared as a decoction for traditional use or applied externally as a wash or poultice for wounds and skin conditions.
Precautions: Use with caution. Scientific evidence supporting its medicinal use is limited. Avoid excessive internal use and use during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless advised by a qualified healthcare professional. Ensure proper plant identification before use.
Botany: Jacaranda is a tree that grows to a height of up to 20 meters. Bark is thin and gray-brown, smooth when young, becoming finely scaly as it ages. Twigs are light reddish-brown, slender and slightly zigzagging. Leaves are large, up to 45 centimeters long, compound, bipinnate, alternately arranged, with several pairs of leaflets. Leaflets are oblong ellipsoidal with parallel venation, an acute apex, and entire margins, i centimeters long. Flowers are tubular shaped, up to 5 centimeters long, grouped in 30 centimeters panicles, in a variety of colors: blue, blur-purple, lilac purple, lavender blue or mauve. Pods follow the flowers, about 5 centimeters in diameter, with numerous, flat and winged seeds, 5 to 6 millimeters long and 4 to 4.5 millimeters wide.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for diarrhea, cough, fever, stomach pain, wounds, and respiratory infections. The roots and bark are commonly used in African traditional medicine.
Preparation: Root or bark is boiled into a decoction and taken in small amounts. Crushed leaves may be applied externally to wounds.
Precautions: Avoid excessive intake because high doses may be toxic. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare provider before use. Use only under proper guidance.
Botany: A thorny evergreen shrub or small tree reaching 3–10 meters tall. It has shiny green leaves, paired thorns, small yellow-green flowers, and reddish-brown edible fruits when mature. Native to Africa.

Symptoms: Commonly used for toothache, mouth ulcers, sore throat, mild pain, inflammation, and digestive discomfort. Known for its natural numbing effect.
Preparation: Fresh leaves or flowers are chewed directly for toothache. Leaves may also be brewed into tea or applied as a paste to affected areas.
Precautions: May cause temporary numbness of the mouth. Avoid excessive consumption. Pregnant women should seek medical advice before use. Individuals allergic to plants in the daisy family should use caution.
Botany: A low-growing annual herb reaching 20–40 cm in height. It has oval green leaves, yellow flower heads with reddish centers, and thrives in warm, humid climates. Native to South America and cultivated throughout tropical regions.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve headaches, colds, cough, nasal congestion, indigestion, stomach cramps, and muscle pain. The leaves are rich in menthol, which provides a cooling sensation.
Preparation: Fresh or dried leaves are steeped in hot water to make herbal tea. Crushed leaves may be inhaled for nasal congestion, or the essential oil (properly diluted) may be applied externally for muscle aches.
Precautions: Avoid ingesting large amounts of essential oil, as it can be toxic. Use diluted oil only for external application. Not recommended for infants or young children due to the strong menthol content. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare provider before use.
Botany: A perennial aromatic herb growing 30–60 cm tall. It has square stems, opposite lance-shaped leaves with serrated margins, and small purple or pale pink flowers. It spreads through underground runners (rhizomes).

Symptoms: Traditionally used for anxiety, stress, insomnia, headaches, mild fever, skin irritation, and wound care. Jasmine flowers are also valued for their calming aroma.
Preparation: Flowers are brewed into herbal tea, while leaves may be crushed into a paste for minor skin problems. Essential oil is commonly used in aromatherapy for relaxation.
Precautions: Essential oil should always be diluted before applying to the skin. Some individuals may experience allergic reactions. Avoid excessive consumption during pregnancy unless advised by a healthcare professional.
Botany: A climbing vine or shrub that grows up to 10 meters long. It has slender green stems, compound leaves, and fragrant white star-shaped flowers that bloom mainly during warm seasons.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for cough, bronchitis, sore throat, digestive problems, urinary tract infections, inflammation, and wound healing. The bark and resin are the most commonly used medicinal parts.
Preparation: Bark is boiled to prepare a decoction for drinking. The resin may be applied externally to minor wounds or used in traditional herbal preparations.
Precautions: Avoid prolonged or excessive use due to limited clinical safety data. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid medicinal use unless recommended by a healthcare professional. People with chronic illnesses should consult a healthcare provider before use.
Botany: A large tropical evergreen tree reaching 20–40 meters in height. It has thick gray-brown bark, glossy compound leaves, fragrant white flowers, and large woody pods containing sweet edible pulp surrounding hard seeds. Native to Central and South America.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for fever, skin diseases, wounds, inflammation, and digestive problems. Leaves and bark are commonly used in folk medicine.
Preparation: Leaves or bark are boiled to prepare a decoction. Crushed leaves may also be applied to minor wounds or skin infections.
Precautions: Seeds should not be eaten raw because they contain toxic compounds. Excessive medicinal use may cause stomach upset. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare provider before use.
Botany: A large deciduous tree growing 20–35 meters tall. It has palmately compound leaves, greenish flowers with a strong odor, and woody pods containing oily seeds.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for fever, stomach pain, inflammation, and minor infections in some Southeast Asian communities.
Preparation: Leaves or bark are boiled into a decoction and consumed in small amounts or used as a wash for affected areas.
Precautions: Limited scientific evidence supports its medicinal use. Use only under professional guidance. Avoid use during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Botany: A small evergreen tree or shrub belonging to the custard apple family (Annonaceae). It has simple glossy leaves, greenish flowers, and fleshy fruits containing several seeds.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for asthma, cough, rheumatism, hepatitis, skin diseases, snake bites, and wound healing.
Preparation: Leaves or roots are boiled into a decoction. Crushed leaves may also be applied externally to wounds and skin infections.
Precautions: Excessive consumption may cause digestive discomfort. Pregnant women should avoid medicinal use unless advised by a healthcare provider.
Botany: A spiny evergreen shrub commonly found in mangrove forests. It grows 1–2 meters tall with glossy, spiny leaves and bluish-purple flowers.

Symptoms: Traditionally used externally for minor skin conditions, although medicinal use is limited due to toxicity.
Preparation: Only external preparations have been reported in traditional medicine. Internal use is not recommended.
Precautions: The fruits and leaves are poisonous if ingested and may cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and neurological symptoms. Keep away from children and pets.
Botany: A small ornamental evergreen shrub growing 30–90 cm tall. It bears white star-shaped flowers followed by bright orange or red berry-like fruits.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for Parkinson's disease symptoms, nerve disorders, infertility, weakness, diabetes, and joint pain. Seeds naturally contain L-DOPA.
Preparation: Seeds are cleaned, roasted, and processed before medicinal use. Powder may be taken in controlled doses under professional supervision.
Precautions: Raw seeds and seed hairs may cause severe itching and irritation. Avoid self-medication due to possible interactions with Parkinson's medications.
Botany: A vigorous climbing vine with trifoliate leaves, purple flowers, and long hairy pods containing dark seeds. It grows in tropical and subtropical regions.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for constipation, fever, hypertension, diabetes, insomnia, and malaria.
Preparation: Young leaves are cooked before consumption, while leaves and bark may be boiled into a decoction.
Precautions: Raw leaves contain compounds that may cause nausea if consumed in large amounts. Excessive intake should be avoided. Pregnant women should consult a healthcare provider.
Botany: A medium-sized evergreen tree growing 10–20 meters tall with compound leaves, yellow flowers, and long brown seed pods. Native to Southeast Asia.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for urinary tract infections, indigestion, bloating, arthritis, and respiratory congestion.
Preparation: Dried berries are brewed as tea or used in herbal extracts. Essential oil is used externally after proper dilution.
Precautions: Avoid prolonged use, especially in people with kidney disease. Not recommended during pregnancy because it may stimulate uterine contractions.
Botany: An evergreen shrub or small tree with needle-like leaves and bluish-purple berry-like cones. It grows naturally in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for urinary tract infections, indigestion, bloating, arthritis, and respiratory congestion.
Preparation: Dried berries are brewed as tea or used in herbal extracts. Essential oil is used externally after proper dilution.
Precautions: Avoid prolonged use, especially in people with kidney disease. Not recommended during pregnancy because it may stimulate uterine contractions.
Botany: An evergreen shrub or small tree with needle-like leaves and bluish-purple berry-like cones. It grows naturally in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to promote bone healing, relieve joint pain, reduce inflammation, and treat hemorrhoids and digestive disorders.
Preparation: Fresh stems are crushed to extract juice or boiled into a decoction. Stem powder is also used in traditional medicine.
Precautions: May cause dry mouth, headache, or digestive discomfort in some individuals. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should seek medical advice before use.
Botany: A succulent climbing vine with thick, four-angled green stems, small leaves, tendrils, and tiny greenish flowers. It is commonly found in tropical and subtropical regions.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for fever, diarrhea, dysentery, skin infections, wounds, and inflammation. The bark and leaves are commonly used in folk medicine.
Preparation: Bark or leaves are boiled to prepare a decoction for drinking or washing wounds. Crushed fresh leaves may also be applied externally to affected areas.
Precautions: Scientific evidence on safety is limited. Avoid excessive use. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare provider before medicinal use.
Botany: A medium to large evergreen tree growing 10–30 meters tall. It has broad glossy leaves, spherical yellow-orange flower heads, and rounded multiple fruits. It is commonly found along rivers and wetlands in Southeast Asia and Australia.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for diarrhea, dysentery, wounds, skin diseases, toothache, inflammation, and fever.
Preparation: Bark is boiled into a decoction for drinking or used as a wash. Crushed bark or leaves may be applied to wounds and skin infections.
Precautions: Avoid prolonged use due to limited clinical evidence. Consult a healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
Botany: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 10–20 meters tall. It has compound leaves, small greenish flowers, and fleshy fruits that turn dark when ripe.

Symptoms: Traditionally used in very small doses as a stimulant and for digestive complaints, weakness, and certain nervous disorders.
Preparation: Seeds are processed extensively in traditional medicine before use because of their toxicity. Medicinal use should only be under expert supervision.
Precautions: Highly toxic. Seeds contain strychnine and brucine, which can cause severe poisoning, convulsions, and death if improperly used. Self-medication is not recommended.
Botany: A large woody climbing vine native to the Philippines. It has glossy opposite leaves, small greenish flowers, and orange fruits containing large, hard seeds known as St. Ignatius beans.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for fever, malaria, diabetes, intestinal worms, inflammation, rheumatism, and digestive disorders.
Preparation: Seeds, leaves, or roots are boiled into a decoction. Leaves may also be crushed and applied externally to swollen or painful areas.
Precautions: Raw seeds may be toxic if consumed in large quantities. Use only recommended doses. Pregnant women should avoid medicinal use unless advised by a healthcare provider.
Botany: A thorny climbing shrub with bipinnate leaves, yellow flowers, and prickly pods containing smooth gray seeds. It grows naturally in coastal and tropical regions.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for cough, colds, stomachache, diarrhea, flatulence, and rheumatism. The bark is valued for its aromatic and medicinal properties.
Preparation: Bark is boiled into a decoction or used as a spice in herbal preparations. Leaves may also be brewed into tea.
Precautions: Excessive intake may irritate the stomach. Essential oil should not be consumed without proper guidance. Individuals with liver disease should use caution due to natural coumarin content.
Botany: A medium-sized evergreen tree endemic to the Philippines. It grows 10–25 meters tall with aromatic bark, simple glossy leaves, and small greenish-yellow flowers followed by dark fruits.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve fever, diarrhea, stomachache, rheumatism, skin infections, inflammation, and wounds. The leaves and roots are commonly used in traditional medicine.
Preparation: Fresh leaves or roots are boiled in water to prepare a decoction that is taken orally for fever and digestive complaints. Crushed leaves may also be applied directly to wounds, boils, and inflamed skin as a poultice.
Precautions: Although Cayratia trifolia has been widely used in traditional medicine, there is limited clinical evidence regarding its long-term safety and effectiveness. Excessive consumption may cause stomach irritation, nausea, or diarrhea. Individuals with chronic liver or kidney disease should seek medical advice before using this plant medicinally. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid medicinal use because adequate safety studies are lacking. Herbal preparations should always be made from properly identified plants to avoid accidental misuse.
Botany: Cayratia trifolia is a perennial climbing vine belonging to the grape family (Vitaceae). It produces slender tendrils that allow it to climb trees, shrubs, and fences. The leaves are compound with three leaflets that are oval to broadly lance-shaped with serrated margins. Small greenish-white flowers develop into clusters of round berries that change from green to dark purple or black when ripe. It commonly grows in grasslands, forests, roadsides, and disturbed areas throughout tropical Asia, including the Philippines.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for joint pain, muscle aches, fever, inflammation, wound healing, and general body weakness. The stems and leaves are the most commonly utilized plant parts.
Preparation: The stems or leaves are boiled to prepare a medicinal decoction that is taken in moderate amounts. Fresh leaves may also be crushed and applied directly to swollen joints, bruises, and minor wounds.
Precautions: There are very few scientific studies confirming the medicinal safety of this species. It should not be used as a replacement for prescribed medications. Excessive intake may lead to digestive discomfort, including stomach cramps or diarrhea. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid medicinal use because its effects on fetal and infant development are unknown. Individuals with existing medical conditions should consult a healthcare professional before taking herbal preparations.
Botany: Tetrastigma harmandii is a vigorous woody climbing vine belonging to the grape family (Vitaceae). It has thick climbing stems with tendrils that enable it to attach to surrounding vegetation. The leaves are compound with three to five leaflets that are glossy green and leathery. Small greenish flowers are produced in clusters and develop into fleshy berries upon maturity. The species naturally occurs in tropical forests of Southeast Asia where it climbs over shrubs and large trees.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for treating wounds, fever, body pain, inflammation, diarrhea, and skin infections. It is also used by some indigenous communities as a general health tonic.
Preparation: Fresh stems or leaves are boiled to prepare a decoction for internal use. Crushed leaves may be applied externally as a poultice to cuts, boils, insect bites, and inflamed skin.
Precautions: Scientific evidence supporting the medicinal use of Tetrastigma loheri remains limited. Excessive intake may result in gastrointestinal discomfort such as nausea or diarrhea. Herbal remedies prepared from this plant should only be used for short periods unless supervised by a qualified healthcare practitioner. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid medicinal use because sufficient safety information is unavailable. Proper identification of the species is important since related vines may have different medicinal properties.
Botany: Tetrastigma loheri is a large woody climbing vine native to the Philippines. It belongs to the grape family (Vitaceae) and grows vigorously in secondary forests and mountainous regions. The plant has compound leaves with several glossy leaflets, branching tendrils, inconspicuous green flowers, and small berry-like fruits. It often climbs to the tops of large trees, forming dense masses of vegetation.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to support the immune system, improve general health, reduce fatigue, aid digestion, and provide antioxidant benefits. It is also consumed as a nutritious edible mushroom.
Preparation: Fresh fruiting bodies are cooked in soups, stews, or stir-fried dishes before consumption. In traditional medicine, dried mushrooms may be boiled to prepare a nourishing broth or herbal soup.
Precautions: This mushroom should only be collected by individuals who are experienced in mushroom identification because poisonous mushrooms may closely resemble edible species. People who are allergic to mushrooms should avoid consuming it. Raw mushrooms should not be eaten because they may cause digestive discomfort. Individuals with weakened immune systems or serious medical conditions should consult a healthcare provider before using mushrooms as herbal supplements.
Botany: Lentinus sajor-caju, commonly known as the oyster mushroom in some regions, is an edible fungus that grows on decaying hardwood logs and tree stumps. It produces shelf-like fruiting bodies with cream to light brown caps, white gills, and short stems. The mushroom plays an important ecological role by decomposing dead wood and recycling nutrients in forest ecosystems. It thrives in warm and humid tropical environments and is also widely cultivated for food.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for urinary problems, fatigue, constipation, cough, and general weakness. The sap, fruits, roots, and young shoots have various medicinal and nutritional uses in traditional medicine.
Preparation: The fresh sap may be consumed after proper processing, while roots are boiled into a decoction for traditional medicinal use. Young shoots and processed fruits are also consumed as food, while other plant parts may be prepared according to traditional practices.
Precautions: Fresh sap ferments rapidly and may become alcoholic if not processed immediately. Some parts of the fruit contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals that can severely irritate the mouth, throat, and skin if eaten without proper preparation. Only properly processed fruits should be consumed. Individuals with diabetes should monitor their intake of palm sugar products prepared from the sap. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before using the plant medicinally.
Botany: Arenga pinnata, commonly known as the sugar palm, is a large solitary palm that can grow between 12 and 20 meters in height. It has a stout trunk covered with black fibrous material and bears large, graceful pinnate leaves that may reach several meters long. Mature trees produce large hanging clusters of flowers followed by rounded fruits containing several seeds. The species is widely distributed throughout Southeast Asia, where it grows in forests, hillsides, and cultivated landscapes. It is highly valued for its sap, fibers, edible fruits, and numerous traditional medicinal and economic uses.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve cough, colds, sore throat, fever, indigestion, stomachache, nausea, headaches, and skin infections. The leaves and fruits are also used to reduce body odor and as a natural insect repellent.
Preparation: The leaves are boiled in water to prepare a decoction or herbal tea for respiratory and digestive ailments. Fresh fruit juice may be diluted and taken in small amounts, while crushed leaves or fruit peels are applied externally to itchy skin, insect bites, or fungal infections. Essential oil extracted from the peel is commonly used in aromatherapy and massage after proper dilution.
Precautions: The juice of Citrus hystrix is highly acidic and may cause stomach irritation when consumed in excessive amounts. Direct application of the juice or essential oil to the skin may increase sensitivity to sunlight (phototoxicity), resulting in irritation or burns after sun exposure. Essential oil should always be diluted before topical use. Individuals with citrus allergies should avoid using this plant. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before using concentrated preparations or essential oils.
Botany: Citrus hystrix, commonly known as kaffir lime or makrut lime, is a small evergreen tree belonging to the Rutaceae family. It usually grows between 2 and 6 meters in height and has thorny branches with distinctive double-lobed, glossy dark green leaves. The tree produces small white fragrant flowers that develop into rough, bumpy green fruits with a thick aromatic rind. It thrives in tropical and subtropical climates and is widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia for both culinary and medicinal purposes.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to treat wounds, burns, cough, fever, kidney stones, urinary tract infections, hypertension, inflammation, boils, and insect bites. It is also valued for its wound-healing and anti-inflammatory properties in many traditional healing systems.
Preparation: Fresh leaves are washed and crushed to extract their juice, which is applied directly to wounds, burns, boils, and insect bites. Leaves may also be boiled to prepare a decoction or infused in hot water to make herbal tea for cough, fever, and urinary problems. Some traditional practices use warmed leaves as a poultice to reduce swelling and pain.
Precautions: Although generally considered safe in traditional medicine when used appropriately, excessive consumption may cause digestive discomfort such as nausea or diarrhea. The plant contains cardiac glycosides, which may be harmful in large quantities and can affect heart function. People with heart disease, kidney disease, or those taking heart medications should consult a healthcare professional before use. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid medicinal use unless recommended by a qualified healthcare provider.
Botany: Bryophyllum pinnatum is a succulent perennial herb belonging to the Crassulaceae family. It grows between 30 and 150 centimeters tall with thick, fleshy green stems and opposite, oval leaves that produce tiny plantlets along their margins. These plantlets easily develop into new plants when they fall to the ground. The plant bears drooping tubular flowers that are greenish, pink, or reddish-purple and thrives in tropical and subtropical regions, especially in moist, well-drained soils.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve diarrhea, dysentery, cough, fever, diabetes, urinary disorders, inflammation, jaundice, and wounds. The leaves, roots, seeds, and flowers are all utilized in various traditional medicinal preparations.
Preparation: Leaves and roots are boiled to prepare a decoction that is taken orally for digestive and urinary complaints. Fresh leaves may be crushed into a paste and applied to wounds, skin infections, and insect bites. The mature seeds are cooked and consumed as food, while young leaves may also be prepared as herbal tea in some traditional practices.
Precautions: Although the seeds are commonly eaten as food, excessive consumption of concentrated herbal preparations may lead to digestive discomfort. Individuals with legume allergies should use caution because allergic reactions may occur. People taking medications for diabetes should monitor their blood sugar levels, as the plant may enhance glucose-lowering effects. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare provider before using the plant medicinally.
Botany: Cajanus cajan, commonly known as pigeon pea, is an erect perennial shrub belonging to the Fabaceae family. It typically grows between 1 and 4 meters tall and has woody stems with trifoliate leaves covered in fine hairs. The plant produces attractive yellow flowers with reddish streaks, followed by elongated seed pods containing several round seeds that vary in color from cream to brown. It is widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions as both a food crop and a medicinal plant because of its adaptability to dry conditions.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to treat fever, cough, sore throat, diarrhea, skin infections, wounds, boils, inflammation, and swollen joints. The leaves, bark, flowers, and roots are commonly used in traditional medicine because of their soothing and anti-inflammatory properties.
Preparation: Fresh leaves are crushed and applied as a poultice to wounds, boils, swollen joints, and inflamed skin. Bark or leaves are boiled into a decoction for cough, fever, and digestive complaints. The flowers may also be prepared as a mild herbal infusion in some traditional practices.
Precautions: Medicinal use of Hibiscus tiliaceus is generally considered safe when used in moderation; however, scientific studies on long-term safety remain limited. Excessive consumption may result in mild digestive discomfort. Individuals who are allergic to plants in the mallow family (Malvaceae) should exercise caution. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should seek medical advice before using medicinal preparations, especially concentrated decoctions.
Botany: Hibiscus tiliaceus, commonly known as sea hibiscus, is a medium-sized evergreen tree belonging to the Malvaceae family. It usually grows between 4 and 10 meters tall and has broad, heart-shaped leaves with soft hairs on the underside. The large yellow flowers have a dark reddish center and gradually change to orange or reddish as they age. It commonly grows along beaches, riverbanks, mangroves, and other coastal environments throughout tropical regions, where it helps stabilize shorelines and prevent soil erosion.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve constipation, indigestion, sore throat, cough, high blood pressure, diabetes, hemorrhoids, and skin inflammation. The fruits, leaves, and latex have been utilized in traditional medicine for centuries because of their nutritional and medicinal properties.
Preparation: The ripe fruits are eaten fresh or dried to improve digestion and relieve constipation. Leaves are boiled to prepare herbal tea or a decoction for diabetes and respiratory ailments. The milky latex has been traditionally applied to warts and certain skin conditions, although it should be used with caution.
Precautions: The milky latex of Ficus carica may cause skin irritation, allergic reactions, or increased sensitivity to sunlight in some individuals. Excessive consumption of the fruits may lead to diarrhea due to their high fiber content. People with latex allergies should avoid direct contact with the plant. Individuals taking medications for diabetes should monitor their blood sugar levels, as fig leaves may have glucose-lowering effects. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before using concentrated herbal preparations.
Botany: Ficus carica, commonly known as the common fig, is a deciduous shrub or small tree belonging to the Moraceae family. It typically grows between 3 and 10 meters in height with smooth gray bark and broad, deeply lobed leaves that exude a white milky latex when cut. The tree produces unique pear-shaped fruits that develop from enclosed flower structures and turn green, purple, or brown when mature. Native to the Mediterranean and Western Asia, it is now cultivated worldwide in warm climates for its edible fruits and medicinal value.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve diarrhea, dysentery, fever, urinary tract infections, skin diseases, wounds, inflammation, and stomach disorders. The leaves, roots, and bark are commonly used in traditional herbal medicine.
Preparation: The leaves, bark, or roots are boiled in water to prepare a decoction that is taken orally for digestive and urinary ailments. Fresh leaves may also be crushed and applied directly to wounds, boils, and inflamed skin to promote healing.
Precautions: Although widely used in traditional medicine, there are limited scientific studies confirming its long-term safety. Excessive intake may cause nausea, diarrhea, or stomach irritation. Individuals with chronic liver or kidney disease should consult a healthcare professional before use. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid medicinal use unless advised by a qualified healthcare provider. Proper identification of the plant is important to prevent confusion with other Phyllanthus species.
Botany: Phyllanthus reticulatus is a thorny evergreen shrub or small tree belonging to the Phyllanthaceae family. It commonly grows between 2 and 6 meters tall with slender branches, small oval leaves arranged alternately along the stems, and tiny greenish-yellow flowers. The fruits are small, round berries that ripen from green to purplish-black. It naturally grows in forests, riverbanks, and open fields throughout tropical Asia, including the Philippines.

Botany: Senna occidentalis is an annual or short-lived perennial shrub belonging to the Fabaceae family. The species is common in roadsides, cultivated land, and open grasslands throughout tropical regions.

Symptoms: Traditionally used to relieve cough, digestive disorders, fever, nervousness, inflammation, urinary complaints, and skin infections. The aromatic seeds are particularly valued for their fragrance and medicinal properties.

Botany: Abelmoschus moschatus, commonly known as musk mallow, is an erect annual or perennial herb belonging to the Malvaceae family. Botany: Carthamus tinctorius, commonly known as safflower, is an annual herb belonging to the Asteraceae family. Botany: Anacardium occidentale, commonly known as cashew, is a medium-sized evergreen tree belonging to the Anacardiaceae family. Botany: Ceriops tagal is a small to medium-sized mangrove tree belonging to the Rhizophoraceae family. Botany: Kalanchoe pinnata is a succulent perennial herb belonging to the Crassulaceae family. Botany: Macaranga tanarius is a fast-growing tree belonging to the Euphorbiaceae family. It commonly reaches heights of 8 to 20 meters and has broad heart-shaped leaves with long stalks. Botany: Sesbania grandiflora, commonly known as vegetable hummingbird or katuray, is a small fast-growing tree belonging to the Fabaceae family. Botany: Xanthostemon verdugonianus, commonly known as mangkono or Philippine ironwood, is a slow-growing evergreen tree belonging to the Myrtaceae family. Botany: Ficus nota, commonly known as tibig, is a medium-sized evergreen tree belonging to the Moraceae family. Botany: Caesalpinia bonduc, commonly known as gray nicker or fever nut, is a large thorny climbing shrub belonging to the Fabaceae family. Botany: Canopy lianas, to 30 m long. Roots fleshy, thickened. Stems terete, to 5 cm in diam.; internodes 2-20 cm; tendrils (3-forked or) simple, to 25 cm. Stipules flattened-triangular, ca. 1 mm; petiole 1-10 cm, glands at blade-petiole junction 2, on concave 2-4 mm in diam. auriculate extensions at apex of petiole in mature leaves, 1-3 mm in diam.; leaf blade ovate to lanceolate, membranous to leathery, glands often present, dotlike, base of mature leaf oblong, unlobed or (2 or)3-lobed with distal 1/3 of leaf often slightly constricted from slight lobation, margin entire to serrate, apex acute to acuminate. Plants (monoecious or) dioecious. Inflorescences often with tendril emerging from center, peduncle to 20 cm, to 40-flowered in males, 2-4-flowered in females; bracts and bracteoles narrowly triangular, ca. 1 mm, apex acute. Pedicel 0.5-13 mm. Flowers tubiform-urceolate, 15-25 × 2-5 mm, including stipe 1-15 mm. Hypanthium urceolate to cupuliform, wall fleshy-leathery, ca. 0.5 mm thick, 3-6 mm deep. Calyx tube 2-3 mm; lobes reflexed, triangular, 1-3 mm, rounded to acute, entire. Petals oblanceolate to triangular, 2-4 × 0.5-1 mm, red punctate, base hastate, apex entire to undulate, rounded to acute. Septa 0.25-3 mm high. Corona absent. Disk glands linear, to 3 mm high, truncate. Male flowers: filaments 1-4 mm, connate up to 2 mm, inserted at base of hypanthium; anthers ca. 3 × 1 mm, acute, up to 0.5 mm apiculate; vestigial ovary ca. 1 mm, gynophore to 1 mm. Female flowers: staminodes 1-3 mm, connate to 1 mm, inserted at base of hypanthium; ovary subglobose to oblong, ca. 4 × 2.5 mm; gynophore ca. 3 mm; style arms ca. 1 mm, free or connate for ca. 0.5 mm; stigmas globose, papillate. Capsules 1-3 per inflorescence, outside deep red at dehiscence, ellipsoid, fruit body to 13 cm, with gynophore to 3 cm, fruit wall leathery. Seeds to 60 per capsule, orbicular; funicles of seeds 5-15 mm.

Symptoms: Traditionally used for fever, cough, inflammation, wounds, skin irritations, menstrual discomfort, and to promote healthy hair growth.

Botany: Herbs to 1.2 m tall, erect, perennial. Stems hirsute, usually 4- or 6-angled. Petiole 3-12 mm; leaf blade ovate to lanceolate, (1-)3-4.5 × (0.5-)1.5-2 cm, abaxially scabrid, adaxially slightly scabrid, base attenuate to broadly cuneate, margin remotely serrulate and slightly ciliate, apex acuminate, acute, or sometimes rounded. Inflorescences of axillary pedunculate cymes with (1-)4(or more) involucres (cymes sometimes branching internally) in axils of leaves or bracts and collectively often forming a terminal leafy panicle-like complex; rachis and inflorescence branches pubescent; outer involucral bracteoles unequal, abaxially pubescent with gland-tipped (sometimes absent) and non-glandular trichomes, larger outer involucral bracteole ± linear, ca. 10 × 2 mm, 1-veined, and apex acute and mucronate, shorter outer involucral bracteole subulate to lanceolate, ca. 6 × 0.1 mm; inner involucral bracteoles narrowly linear to subulate, unequal in length. Calyx lobes lanceolate, ca. 3 mm, outside sparsely pubescent with non-glandular trichomes, inside sparsely pubescent with sessile gland-tipped trichomes, margin membranous at base, apex long acuminate. Corolla light to dark purple, ca. 1 cm, outside pubescent with non-glandular trichomes; tube basally cylindric for ca. 5 mm; lip in lower position narrowly elliptic, 5-7 × 1-2 mm, apex emarginate; lip in upper position elliptic, 3-7 × 2-3 mm, 3-lobed. Staminal filaments ca. 5 mm, white hairy; anther thecae ovoid, superposed, not touching. Ovary ovoid, pubescent and glandular; style glabrous; stigma 2-lobed. Capsule 0.9-1.3 cm, pubescent with non-glandular trichomes. Seeds 2.2-2.5 mm, rough and tuberculate.

Symptoms: Traditionally used in some folk practices for fever, headaches, skin conditions, and inflammation, though its medicinal use is limited and not well established.

Flowers nocturnal, fragrant. Sepals elliptic to ovate, ± leathery, glabrous; outer 3 sepals 5-12 mm, apex with a stout spreading awn 4-9 mm; inner 2 sepals 7-15 mm, mucronate. Corolla white, with greenish bands, salverform; tube 7-12 cm, ca. 5 mm in diameter; limb 7-12 cm in diameter, shallowly 5-undulate. Stamens exserted; filaments inserted in apical 1/2 of corolla tube, glabrous; anthers sagittate basally. Pistil exserted; ovary narrowly conical, glabrous. Stigma 2-lobed. Capsule ovoid, 2.5-3 cm, apiculate. Seeds white, brown, or black, 7-8 mm, glabrous. (Flora of China @ efloras.org)

Botany: Melodinus fusiformis is a woody liana that grows as a stout climber, reaching lengths of up to 10 m. Five indistinct corona scales are present, exserted and villous with 2- or 3-cleft apices. Five stamens have included filaments inserted near the base of the corolla tube. Superior ovary is 2-loculed with numerous ovules, topped by a short style and a pistil head with dilated, 2-cleft apex serving as the stigma. Fruits are fusiform berries, 3.5–5.3 cm long and 2.2–4 cm wide, containing numerous seeds embedded in pulp. Seeds lack a coma.

Flowers are about 6 millimeters long, reddish purple, crowded in axillary racemes which are 6 to 20 centimeters long. Pods are straight, reflexed, 1.5 to 2.5 centimeters long, about 2.5 millimeters wide, covered with browns, spreading hairs, containing 4 to 6 seeds.

Botany: A slender vine not exceeding a stem diameter of 2 cm. Leaves: Leaf blades about 12-55 x 3-12 mm, petioles absent or about 0.5-1 mm long. Flowers: Pedicels about 8-10 mm long. Sepals, glabrous, ovate or narrowly ovate, about 4-6 x 2 mm. Corolla trumpet-shaped, about 8-12 x 7-12 mm. Stamens about 5 mm long. Ovary globose, about 0.6-0.7 mm diam. Style about 5-5.5 mm long. Stigmas 2, globose, surface pappilose. Ovules 2 per locule. Fruits: Fruits globose, about 5 x 5-7 mm, enveloped by the persistent sepals. Seeds up to 4 per fruit, each seed angular, about 4 x 3 mm, shaped like an orange segment. Cotyledons bilobed, crumpled and folded in a complex fashion with lenses of endosperm between the folds. Radicle curved, about 2-6 mm long.

Botany: Kalancho integra is an herb, perennial, 40-120 cm tall, glabrous. Inflorescences cymose, ca. 10 cm, elongated in fruit; bracts linear. Sepals linear-ovate to narrowly triangular, apex acuminate. Corolla yellow, 1.5-2 cm; lobes acuminate at apex. Stamens inserted at corolla throat; filaments short. Nectar scales linear, ca. 3 mm. (Flora of China)

Botany: Sambong is a half woody, strongly aromatic shrub, densely and softly hairy, 1 to 4 meters high. Stems grow up to 2.5 centimeters in diameter. Leaves are simple, alternate, elliptic- to oblong-lanceolate, 7 to 20 centimeters long, toothed at the margins, pointed or blunt at the tip, narrowing to a short petiole which are often auricled or appendaged. Flowering heads are stalked, yellow and numerous, 6 to 7 millimeters long, and borne on branches of a terminal, spreading or pyramidal leafy panicle. Discoid flowers are of two types: peripheral ones tiny, more numerous, with tubular corolla; central flowers few, large with campanulate corolla. Involucral bracts are green, narrow and hairy. Anther cells tailed at base. Fruits are achenes, dry, 1-seeded, 10-ribbed, hairy at top.

Botany: Kalumbibit is a prickly shrub or woody vine reaching a length of 10 meters or more. Leaves are bipinnate, often nearly 1 meter long, with the rachis armed with stout, sharp, recurved spines. Pinnae usually number about 10 pairs and are about 20 centimeters long with a pair of short, sharp spines at the point of attachment of each pair of leaflets. Leaflets also number about 10 pairs and are oblong, 2 to 5 centimeters long and somewhat hairy. Flowers are yellow, borne in axillary, simple or panicled racemes and about 1 centimeter long. Calyx is deeply cleft, the disk basal, the lobes imbricate, the lowest one larger than the others. Petals spreading, usually clawed, the uppermost smaller than the others. Stamens, 10, free, declinate, anthers versatile. Ovary few-ovuled. Fruits are pods, oblong 5 to 7 centimeters in length, inflated and covered with slender spines and contain one or two seeds. The seeds are large, somewhat rounded or ovoid, hairy, gray and shiny.

Botany: Calophyllum soulattri is a tree. Twigs fine tomentulose. Leaves oblong or narrowly ovate, 10-20 cm long, 3-7 cm wide, apically short acuminate into a drip tip, basally obtuse, the costa elevated or plane above, elevated beneath to the tip, sparingly puberulent, lateral veins evident, ribs (veins plus ducts) 39-40 per cm, the margins mostly not drying revolute, petioles 1-1.5 cm long, drying dark, minutely tomentose, grooved above. Inflorescences short cymes fasciculate in the leaf axils, crowded, the peduncle basally pubescent, bracts wanting, bracteoles obsolete; pedicels ca. 1.5 cm long, glabrous, slender. Flowers perfect, sepals 2; petals 2(-3), ca. 8 mm long, rotund, apically ciliolate; stamens 60-100 (Stevens, 1976), the filaments ca. 3 mm long, basally connate, the anthers oblong, ca. 2 mm long; ovary glabrous, the style ca. 3 mm long, the stigma peltate. Fruit ovoid to globose, ca. 10 mm across, sometimes apiculate, drying brown, often glaucous, more or less smooth. This species is recognizable by the very numerous ribs of the leaves and by the small fruit. (Flora de Panama)

Botany: Dama de noche is an erect and climbing ornamental smooth shrub, about 2 to 3 meters in height, with long often-drooping branches. Leaves are oblong-ovate to oblong-lanceolate, 8 to 10 centimeters long, pointed at the tips. Flowers are numerous, slender, yellowish-green, about 2 to 2.3 centimeters long, borne in lax, axillary and terminal inflorescences, 7 to 10 centimeters long.

Botany: Nipa is a monoecious palm, with stout, subterranean, trunkless and thornless rootstock. Leaves are at the ends of the rootstocks, large, rosette and compound, 5 to 10 meters long, arising from the stout underground stem (rhizome). Leaflets are numerous, rigid, lanceolate, up to 1 meter long, 2 to 7 cm centimeters wide. Male inflorescence is brown, erect, up to 1 meter high. Female inflorescence is stout, 1 meter high or less. Fruit is globose, nodding, up to 30 centimeters in diameter. Carpels are numerous, dark-brown, striate, smooth, 10 to 14 centimeters long, compressed, obovate. Seeds are hard, white, and as large as a hen's egg.

Botany: Possibly annual herb, usually 30–60 cm high, with fine pale ± appressed hairs to ± cottony. Heads solitary, terminal on main and side branches, usually subtended by 1-several small leaves and nodding. Outer involucral bracts spreading or reflexed, lanceolate or elliptic, acute, entire, pubescent; inner bracts narrow-oblong, acute, obtuse or rounded, margins often slightly toothed, erect. Florets yellow. Achenes c. 4 mm long. (New South Wales Flora Online)

Heads globose, becoming somewhat lengthened, with 3-7-flowered cymes; rachis 0.2-3.5 cm, glabrous or pubescent. Bracts and bracteoles ovate-lanceolate, 3-5 mm, white on margin and with green or purple (?red) midvein, apex long acuminate. Tepals obliquely spreading at anthesis, later erect, ovate-lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate, 4-5 mm. Stamens 5; filaments connate at base. Ovary ovoid, glabrous; style nearly as long as filaments. Utricles enclosed in persistent perianth, pale green, ovoid, 3-3.5 mm in diam., dehiscent by lid. Seeds 1.5-2 mm in diam. (Flora of China)

Botany: Cynometra cauliflora is a shrub or a small evergreen tree very ramified, that usually does not exceed the 8 m of height, with brown-grayish bark. The leaves, on a 0,4-0,8 cm long petiole, are alternate, formed by two oblong-ovate leaflets, asymmetric with respect to the central rib, with obtuse or slightly pointed apex and entire margins, 6-15 cm long and 2-5 cm broad, of glossy dark green color above, pale green below, coriaceous; the young leaves, of bright pink color, drooping, are particularly ornamental. The inflorescences are short compact racemes grouped at the nodes of the trunk or of the main branches, often close to the ground, with small bisexual flowers, of about 0,8 cm of diameter, with calyx usually quadripartite with white-pinkish lobes, about 0,4 cm long and broad, retroflexed, 5 thin white or white-pinkish lanceolate petals, about 0,4 cm long, 8-10 stamina and about 0,5 cm long style. The fruits are reniform legumes with yellowish pulp, edible, 5-10 cm long, 4-5 cm broad and 1,2-3 cm thick, with wrinkly surface of brown green color turning greenish yellow when ripe, containing one seed only, 3,5-6 cm long.

Botany: Cyperus rotundus is a slender, erect, glabrous, perennial grasslike plant, 10 to 40 centimeters high. Rhizomes or underground stems are wiry, bearing black, hard, ovoid tubers which are about 1 centimeter in diameter. Ground stems are usually solitary, distinctly 3-angled above. Leaves are 5 to 15 centimeters long, sometimes as long as the stems, about 3 millimeters wide, and narrowly linear. Umbel is simple or compound, 2 to 6 centimeters long, with 2 to 8 unequal primary rays. Spikes are dense or rather lax. Spikelets are 3 to 8, 10 to 25 millimeters long, brown, slender, with 10 to 25 florets in each spikelet, linear, and slightly compressed. Rachilla of the spikelet distinctly winged. Glumes are 2.5 to 3 millimeters long, closely or loosely imbricate. Glumes of the floret distichously arranged, the first 2 empty, the third one bisexual. Fruit is an achene, obovoid or oblong, black or granulate, 3-angled, one-seeded, covered with a scurfy bloom

Botany: Myristica fragrans is an evergreen tree, usually 5–15 m (16–49 ft) tall, but occasionally reaching 20 m (66 ft) or even 30 m (98 ft) on Tidore. Alternately arranged leaves are dark green, 5–15 cm (2.0–5.9 in) long by 2–7 cm (0.8–2.8 in) wide with petioles about 1 cm (0.4 in) long. Species is dioecious, i.e. "male" or staminate flowers and "female" or carpellate flowers are borne on different plants, although occasional individuals produce both kinds of flower. Flowers are bell-shaped, pale yellow and somewhat waxy and fleshy. Staminate flowers are arranged in groups of one to ten, each 5–7 mm (0.2–0.3 in) long; carpellate flowers are in smaller groups, one to three, and somewhat longer, up to 10 mm (0.4 in) long. Carpellate trees produce smooth yellow ovoid or pear-shaped fruits, 6–9 cm (2.4–3.5 in) long with a diameter of 3.5–5 cm (1.4–2.0 in). Fruit has a fleshy husk. When ripe the husk splits into two halves along a ridge running the length of the fruit. Inside is a purple-brown shiny seed, 2–3 cm (0.8–1.2 in) long by about 2 cm (0.8 in) across, with a red or crimson covering (an aril). Seed is the source of nutmeg; the aril the source of mace.

Precautions: Danger: Highly toxic. The seeds and other parts of the plant contain strychnine and brucine, which can cause severe muscle spasms, seizures, respiratory failure, and death if ingested. Botany: Strychnine plant is a medium-sized, deciduous tree, growing to a height of 10 meters, with a straight, thick trunk. Leaves are leathery, smooth, opposite, entire, shiny, broadly elliptic or ovate, 7.5 to 15 centimeters long and 6 to 8 centimeters wide, 5-nerved, blunt or rounded at the base, and pointed at the tip. Flowers are greenish-white, numerous, small, and borne on small, terminal hairy cymes 2.5 to 5 centimeters in diameter. Calyx is small, with 5 teeth. Corolla is tubular or funnel-shaped, with 5 reflexed, short limbs. Fruit is a berry, smooth, indehiscent, orange when mature, round and 3 to 5 centimeters in diameter. Rind is a shell-like pulp with 2 to 5 seeds embedded in it. Seeds are disc-shaped, nearly flat, 10 to 30 millimeters in diameter, 4 to 6 millimeters thick, shining, light silvery-grey, and covered with closely appressed hairs, odorless but quite bitter.

Leaflets are numerous, linear-lanceolate, nearly 1 meter long, 2 to 4 centimeters wide. Male inflorescence is dense, having numerous, cylindric spikes which are 7 to 12 centimeters long and about 1 centimeter in diameter; the rachises excurrent as a stout awn. Female inflorescence is dense, branched, 20 to 30 centimeters long, the flowers densely disposed. Fruit is borne in large dense masses.

The flowers are tiny, only reaching 0.61 centimeters (0.24 in) in diameter, white, and do not begin to appear until the tree has reached a few years of age. The fruits it produces are small, opaque and fleshy. The bark is light gray/brown and is corrugated.

Precautions: Generally safe when consumed as food. Excessive consumption may cause digestive discomfort in some individuals. Botany: Okra is a coarse, erect, branched, more or less hairy, annual herb, 0.6 to 1.5 meters high. Leaves are long-petioled, orbicular or orbicular-ovate, about 25 centimeters long or less; with a heart-shaped base; the margins, 3- to 5-lobed. Petioles are equal to the blade in length or longer. Flowers are axillary and solitary; corolla, large and yellow, and inside, deep purple at the base. Fruit is elongated, 10 to 25 centimeters long, 1.5 to 3 centimeters in diameter, tapering to a blunt point and containing rows of rounded, kidney shaped seeds.

Fruits globular, about 2.5-3 centimeters diam. Seeds about 1.8 x 1.8 centimeters. Embryo located near the apex of the seed. Embryo small, about 2 millimeters long, swollen about the middle. Cotyledons about as wide as the radicle.

Botany: Grey mangroves is a shrub or tree growing to a height of 3 to 10 m (9.8 to 32.8 ft), or up to 14 meters (46 ft) in tropical regions. Habit is a gnarled arrangement of multiple branches. Bark is smooth, light-grey, with thin, stiff, brittle flakes, sometimes whitish, as referred to in the common name. Leaves are thick, 5 to 8 cm (2.0 to3.1 in) long, bright and glossy green on the upper surface, silvery-white or grey, with very small matter hairs on the surface below. Aerial roots (pneumatophores) grow to a height of about 20 cm (7.9 in), and a diameter of 1 cm (0.39 in), which allow the plant to absorb oxygen that is deficient in the habitat. Roots anchor the plant during sea water inundation in soft substrate of tidal systems. Flowers are white to golden yellow, less than a centimeter (0.39 in) across, occurring in clusters of three to five. Fruit contains large cotyledons that surround the new stem of a seedling.

Precautions: Generally safe when consumed as food. Excessive consumption may cause stomach irritation, heartburn, or bloating in sensitive individuals. Stamens 15; filaments short, unequal; anthers oblong; connective appendages short, obtuse. Ovary globose, densely puberulous; style short; stigma capitate. Botany: Kaong or sugar palm is a palm tree, with a stout trunk with distinct annular scars, growing to a height of 12 to 15 meters, with a diameter of about 40 centimeters. Leaflets are up to 100 or more on each side, linear, 1 to 1.5 meters long, the tip lobed and variously toothed, the base 2-auricled, the lower surface white or pale. Inflorescence is axillary with stout, decurved peduncle, the pendulous branches very numerous, up to1.5 meters long. Male flowers are in pairs, about 12 millimeters long. Fruits are rounded or depressed rounded, about 5 centimeters in diameter, containing 2 to 3 seeds.

Botany: Cerbera odollam is a dicotyledonous angiosperm, a medium-sized tree up to about 12 meters high, with a round and bushy crown. The branches whorled around the trunk. Flowers are large, with a funnel-shaped corolla, five-lobed. Fruit, when green, resembles a small mango. It as a thick green fibrous husk enclosing an ovoid kernel which measures about 2 centimeters by 1.5 centimeters, with two cross-matching white fleshy halves. On exposure to air, the kernel turns violet to dark grey to brown or black.

Botany: Pantug-pantugan is an erect, branched, hairy annual herb, growing 0.5 to 0.8 meter high. The branches are terete and often tinged with purple, the ultimate ones slightly angular. Flowers are solitary, axillary, about 8 millimeters long. Corolla is pale yellow, with 5 large, purple spots at the base inside. Fruit is round, fleshy and edible, about 1 centimeter in diameter. Calyx is inflated, accrescent, and ovoid, about 3 centimeters long, 2 centimeters in diameter, green, with 5 prominent and alternating slender and purplish ribs.

Fruit an oblong-ovoid capsule, 3.5-6 cm × 2-2.5 cm, hairy, usually 5-angled and splitting into 5 segments. Seeds numerous, spherical to reniform, 2-4 mm in diameter, black.

Botany: Toona sureni is a medium-sized to large tree, reaching a maximum height of around 40 to 60 m (130 to 200 ft) and a diameter of 100 to 300 cm (39 to 118 in). Bole possesses buttress roots up to a height of 2 m (6.6 ft) and remains unbranched and straight up to a height of 20 to 30 m (66 to 98 ft). Bark is fibrous and flaky in texture with numerous vertical fissures. It is pale brown to whitish or grayish brown in color. When cut, the bark and sapwood produce a pleasant odor reminiscent of cinnamon. Sap is colorless and does not change in color after being exposed to air. Sapwood of Toona sureni is white to pinkish or light red in color, while the heartwood is light red or brown. Leaves are pinnate and large, with a length of about 29 to 84 cm (11 to 33 in). They are arranged spirally, usually clustered at the ends of twigs. Leaflets are lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate in shape, arranged somewhat opposite each other, usually in pairs of 6 to 9, with a maximum of 12 pairs. Upper and lower surfaces of the leaflet midribs are characteristically hairy (pilose). Inflorescences are terminal, occurring at the tips of branchlets, paniculate and pendant, reaching a length of around 40 cm (16 in). Individual flowers are small (around 4 to 5 mm (0.16 to 0.20 in) in length), and are sweetly fragrant. Flowers are individually unisexual, though both male and female flowers occur in the same plant. Fruits are leathery capsules, around 25 mm (0.98 in) long and brown in color, each containing more than 100 seeds. Seeds are narrow and usually 11 to 20 mm (0.43 to 0.79 in) in length, with a maximum length of 22 mm (0.87 in); and 1 to 10 mm (0.039 to 0.394 in) in diameter, and winged at both ends (subequal).

Botany: Kayali is a densely tufted, sympodial bamboo. Botany: An evergreen tree that grows some 10-20m tall in Southeast Asia, 3-15m tall in Zhongguo, China. Petals are 6-8, orbicular, when fully grown around 2-3mm in diameter, more or less cohering (largely as the apices of all petals fold into a cylinder at the center between the staminal filaments). Each locule has about 9-16 ovules. The rather stout style is some 3-8mm long, the same or slightly longer than the stamens. The edible fruit is of variable shape, from cylindrical to turbinate to pyriform, often galled and irregular, excavated at the apex, and when mature 11-14 by 9-10 mm in size. Calyx lobes are not obvious. The pericarp is succulent. Cells radiate from the endocarp to the exocarp. Seeds are about 7-8 by 7-8mm, with the testa apparently absent. The seedlings have about 3 pairs of reduced leaves, cataphylls, and before the first pair of true leave appear, these cataphylls are some present between the leaves at later stages. At the tenth leaf stage, conspicuously quadrangled or shortly winged twigs appear, with a lanceolate to ovate leaf, whose apex is acuminate to acute, and a cuneate base. Oil dots are numerous, just visible to the naked eye, clearly visible with a hand-lens. Seeds germinate between 38-95 days.

Precautions: Use with caution. The plant contains calcium oxalate crystals, which can cause mouth and throat irritation, burning sensation, swelling, nausea, and digestive discomfort if ingested. Avoid consuming any part of the plant. Handle sap carefully as it may irritate sensitive skin. Keep away from children and pets. Ensure proper plant identification before any medicinal use.
Botany: Zu zu plant is an evergreen plant that grows from a stout underground, succulent water-storing rhizome, attaining a height of 45 to 60 centimeters. Leaves are pinnate, 40 to 60 centimeters long, with 6-8 pairs of leaflets 7 to 15 centimeters long, smooth, shiny and dark green. Flowers are small bright yellow to brown on bronze spadix 5 centimeters long, partly hidden among the leaf bases.
